archetype.name: Pocket Passer (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A big-framed, 11-year veteran who plays from the pocket, works the middle and intermediate levels well when he gets the ball out, and now sits behind Kyler Murray as a spot starter and emergency relief.

report.headline: Efficient in short relief, but the sacks are a long-running habit
report.take:
Carson Wentz's 2026 comes down to two games and 48 dropbacks. He came on for Kyler Murray in Week 1, played 83% of the snaps and threw three touchdowns against Green Bay. He then started Week 2 in a 9-3 grinder at Chicago. Murray has started every game since, and the depth chart lists Wentz as QB2. Read his line as a measure of what Minnesota gets if he is pressed into duty again, not as a starter's season.

The results look better than the process. His 8.24 adjusted net yards per dropback ranks 12th of 45 and his 7.7% TD rate ranks 5th, with no interceptions. Underneath that, his completion rate over expected is -7.79 (41st), his bad-throw rate is 20.5% (last among charted passers), and his 13.3% sack rate is dead last. The value came in a narrow band. He averaged 0.894 EPA a throw over the middle against 0.038 to the left. Throws of 10+ air yards produced 0.673 EPA per attempt against 0.133 underneath. Justin Jefferson's 14 targets added 13.0 EPA, and three deep attempts added 5.1 of the total. That is a few big completions to an elite receiver carrying an otherwise shaky set of throws. The Week 1 relief outing (5.0 EPA) did most of the lifting, and the Week 2 start managed only 0.5.

The sacks are not noise, and the inaccuracy probably isn't either. His pressure-to-sack rate sits at 66.7%, after 39.6% last year (46th of 62), 37.1% in Washington and 33.6% in his final Philadelphia year. He is pressured only 20% of the time, about middle of the pack, so the problem is what happens once a rusher arrives: he holds the ball looking for something downfield instead of throwing it away. The CPOE collapse is a different story. He was +1.1 last season and has hovered just below zero for most of his career, so the -8.9 swing on 39 attempts should mostly come back. Without a lot of help, he plays like a league-average passer with a sack problem.

The environment explains why Minnesota can win with him anyway. The Vikings field the No. 1 defense in EPA, success rate and sack rate, and their offense ranks 27th in EPA and last in success rate. The plan when he plays is to avoid giving games away, and his zero turnovers and 2-0 record fit that. The supporting cast is thinning, though. Left guard Donovan Jackson is on IR, left tackle Christian Darrisaw is questionable with a concussion, and Hockenson, Addison and Josh Oliver are all banged up or out. For a passer whose main flaw is taking sacks, a weaker line is the worst kind of attrition.

strengths.title: Wins in the intermediate middle
strengths.body: His throws of 10+ air yards produced 0.673 EPA per attempt, and throws over the middle 0.894, with near-normal accuracy on that tenPlus band. That is where his size and arm still play: driving the ball between the hashes to Jefferson and Hockenson. It is a small sample, but it matches what he did in his better Philadelphia and Indianapolis seasons.

strengths.title: Ball security so far
strengths.body: He has no interceptions on 39 attempts, the best intPct rank possible, and no lost fumbles. Some of that is luck: he threw five picks in five games last season and has one turnover-worthy fumble this year. Still, it fits the low-risk role a backup plays behind a top defense.

strengths.title: Production per dropback despite sacks
strengths.body: Even after absorbing the sacks, he sits 12th in adjusted net yards per dropback and 19th in EPA per dropback. Three touchdowns in a quarter-and-change of Week 1 relief pushed his TD rate to 5th. Expect regression, since the TD rate rests on three scores, but the per-play efficiency is roughly in line with his 2025 7.2 YPA.

concerns.title: Sacks are a career trait now
concerns.body: A 13.3% sack rate ranks last of 45, and two-thirds of his pressures end in sacks. That is not new: his pressure-to-sack rate ranked 46th last season and has been poor in most years since 2020. It reflects a habit of hunting downfield rather than throwing it away, and with his starting left guard on IR and his left tackle concussed, it is unlikely to fix itself.

concerns.title: Accuracy has fallen off
concerns.body: His CPOE is -7.79 (41st), down 8.9 points from last year. His 20.5% bad-throw rate is the worst among charted passers, and short throws came in at a -12.2 CPOE. Part of this is a 39-attempt sample, and his career sits near zero, so expect drift back toward about -2. His bad-throw rates have ranked poorly for years, though, so he won't become accurate.

concerns.title: Thin cast if he plays
concerns.body: Outside Jefferson and Hockenson, the targets have been costly: Addison's seven targets lost 3.9 EPA. Hockenson was ruled out last week with a concussion, and Addison is questionable with a hamstring. Oliver is on IR. Without Hockenson in particular, the middle-of-the-field game that carried him narrows to one receiver.

trend.note: He posted 5.0 passing EPA in Week 1 relief and 0.5 in the Week 2 start, taking three sacks in each. He hasn't thrown a pass since Murray reclaimed the job in Week 3.

nextGame.headline: Soft Colts pass rush suits him, if he plays
nextGame.body:
Indianapolis is the right kind of opponent for Wentz's specific flaw. The Colts rank 29th in QB hit rate and 22nd in sack rate, and they just lost edge rusher Arden Key to IR. A defense that can't get home won't cash in on his tendency to hold the ball. Their pass defense is 20th in EPA and 23rd on short throws. The caveat is the top of their coverage: Colts opponents' WR1s have managed only 0.05 EPA a target (4th-stingiest). Sauce Gardner, the likely reason, is doubtful with a calf strain, which would open things up for Jefferson. Minnesota is a 6.5-point home favorite with a 41.5 total, indoors, so a low-volume, lead-protecting script is the likely shape.

The real question is whether he plays at all. Murray has started every game since Week 2, the depth chart lists Wentz as QB2, and the dossier shows no injury listing for Murray. So Wentz's outlook is a backup's: zero most likely, a quality spot if Murray goes down. On Minnesota's side, Darrisaw's concussion and Hockenson's status matter most. A backup tackle against a weak rush is survivable; losing Hockenson removes his second-best target over the middle.

keyMatchups.title: His sack habit vs. weak rush
keyMatchups.body: The Colts are 29th in QB hit rate and 22nd in sack rate, and Key is on IR. That is the best possible opponent for a passer who converts two-thirds of his pressures into sacks. If the pocket stays clean, his intermediate game has room.

keyMatchups.title: Jefferson vs. Gardner-less secondary
keyMatchups.body: Colts opponents' WR1s have averaged just 0.05 EPA a target against them. Gardner, an 89%-snap corner, is doubtful. Jefferson produced most of Wentz's value this season, so Gardner's absence would matter most here.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's patched left side
keyMatchups.body: Jackson is on IR and Darrisaw is questionable with a concussion. A weak Colts rush limits the damage, but the line is the swing factor for any Wentz snaps.

nextGame.watch: Whether Murray takes every snap. If Wentz enters, watch whether he gets the ball out against a rush that rarely hits the quarterback.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect Wentz to spend most of the remaining season holding a clipboard. His fantasy and box-score value is near zero unless Murray misses time. If he does start, the template is Week 2: a low-volume game behind the league's best defense, around 20 attempts, few turnovers and too many sacks. His 51-sack pace17 isn't literal, but it shows the problem. Plan on something like 160-230 passing yards and roughly one touchdown per start, with two to four sacks.

The interception-free run and the top-five TD rate will regress, since they rest on 39 attempts and three touchdowns, two of them in a single relief burst. The CPOE should recover toward his career norm of slightly below zero. The sack rate should ease from historic levels but stay bottom-tier, because it has been for most of the last six seasons. The supporting cast will shape the details: a healthy Hockenson and Darrisaw make him a competent fill-in, while further line attrition turns him into a liability the defense has to cover for.

confidence.note: Only 48 dropbacks across two games; he is the backup with no starting role.
